This module contains all of the logic for paths.\n4. //!\n5. //! Paths can be thought of as similar to file paths (in an operating system) pointing\n6. //! to specific files inside of a directory.\n7. //! A `Value` is a data structure that can contain recursively nested fields. Paths\n8. //! allow referring to a specific field inside of a `Value`.\n9. //!\n10. //! # Example\n11. //! Below is a sample `Value`. Different fields can be accessed with paths.\n12. //! ```json\n13. //! {\n14. //!   \"foo\": {\n15. //!       \"bar\": 1\n16. //!    },\n17. //!    \"baz\": [\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"]\n18. //! }\n19. //! ```\n20. //!\n21. //! | path   | value it points to                    |\n22. //! |--------|---------------------------------------|\n23. //! | `.foo.bar` | `1`\n24. //! | `.foo` | `{ \"bar\": 1 }`\n25. //! | `.`    | `{ \"foo\" : { \"bar\" : 1 }, \"baz\" : [\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"] }`\n26. //! | `.baz[0]` | `\"a\"`\n27. //! | `.baz` | `[\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"]`\n28. //!\n29. //!\n30. //! # Traits\n31. //! There are 2 main traits that define a path. Most functions that use a path for querying\n32. //! will require one of these traits, rather than a concrete type.\n33. //!\n34. //! - [ValuePath] is a path that points to a field inside of a `Value`.\n35. //! - [TargetPath] is a path that points to a field inside of a `target`. A `target` in VRL refers to\n36. //! the external data being processed by a VRL script. A `target` has two main sections that can be\n37. //! pointed to, `event` and `metadata`.  [TargetPath::prefix] identifies the section, and\n38. //! [TargetPath::value_path] is a [ValuePath] pointing into that section.\n39. //!\n40. //! Note that for performance reasons, since [ValuePath] and [TargetPath] require [Clone], these\n41. //! traits are only implemented on types that are cheap to clone (usually references). That means\n42. //! when passing in a value (e.g. [OwnedValuePath]) into a function that requires `impl ValuePath`,\n43. //! it will generally need to be passed in as a reference.\n44. //!\n45. //! # Owned Paths\n46. //! [OwnedValuePath] and [OwnedTargetPath] are pre-parsed paths. That means that accessing fields\n47. //! using an owned path is very fast. There is an upfront cost however, since owned paths are parsed\n48. //! when they are created, and the segments are heap allocated. Owned paths should be preferred\n49. //! if they can be created when performance isn't as much of a concern (e.g. startup time)\n50. //! and they can be stored for re-use.\n51. //! Owned paths tend to be easier to work with since you can directly access / manipulate the\n52. //! segments that make up the path.\n53. //!\n54. //! If a path is being created and will only be used once, it may make sense to use other types.\n55. //! For example here are two different ways to append a segment to a [OwnedValuePath]  before querying\n56. //! a `Value`:\n57. //! - Use [OwnedValuePath::with_field_appended] to create a new [OwnedValuePath] and use that. This\n58. //! method is preferred if the new path will be used multiple times and the path adjustment can be\n59. //! done in a non performance-critical part of the code (e.g. at startup).\n60. //! - Use [ValuePath::concat] which con concatenate two [ValuePath]'s very efficiently without\n61. //! allocating on the heap.\n62. //!\n63. //! To convert a string into an owned path, use either [parse_value_path] or [parse_target_path].\n64. //!\n65. //! # String Paths\n66. //! [ValuePath] and [TargetPath] are implemented for [&str]. That means a raw / unparsed string can\n67. //! be used as a path. This use is discouraged, and may be removed in the future. It mostly\n68. //! exists for backwards compatibility in places where String paths are used instead of owned paths.\n69. //! Using string paths is slightly slower than using an owned path. It's still very fast\n70. //! but it is easy to introduce bugs since some compile-time type information is missing -\n71. //! such as whether it is a target vs value path, or if the entire string is meant\n72. //!  to be treated as a single segment vs being parsed as a path.\n73. //!\n74. //! # Macros\n75. //! Several macros exist to make creating paths easier. These are used if the structure of the\n76. //! path being created is already known. <strong>The macros do not parse paths</strong>. Use\n77. //! [parse_value_path] or [parse_target_path] instead if the path needs to be parsed.\n78. //!\n79. //! You need to pass in each segment into the macro as separate arguments. A single argument is treated as\n80. //! a single segment. This is true for all of the path macros.\n81. //!\n82. //! For example, [owned_value_path!][crate::owned_value_path] can be used to easily created owned paths.\n83. //! - `owned_value_path!(\"foo.bar\", \"x\")` will create a path with *two* segments. Equivalent to `.\"foo.bar\".x`\n84. //!\n85. \n86. mod borrowed;\n87. mod concat;\n88. mod jit;\n89. mod owned;\n90. \n91. use self::jit::JitValuePath;\n92. use snafu::Snafu;\n93. use std::fmt::Debug;\n94. \n95. pub use borrowed::BorrowedSegment;\n96. pub use concat::PathConcat;\n97. pub use owned::{OwnedSegment, OwnedTargetPath, OwnedValuePath};\n98. \n99. #[derive(Clone, Debug, Eq, PartialEq, Snafu)]\n100. pub enum PathParseError {\n101.     #[snafu(display(\"Invalid field path {:?}\", path))]\n102. ($($segment:expr),*) => {{\n111.            &[$($crate::path::BorrowedSegment::from($segment),)*]\n112.     }};\n113. }\n114. \n115. /// Syntactic sugar for creating a pre-parsed path.\n116. /// This path points at an event (as opposed to metadata).\n117. #[macro_export]\n118. macro_rules! event_path {\n119.     ($($segment:expr),*) => {{\n120.            ($crate::path::PathPrefix::Event, &[$($crate::path::BorrowedSegment::from($segment),)*])\n121.     }};\n122. }\n123. \n124. /// Syntactic sugar for creating a pre-parsed path.\n125. /// This path points at metadata (as opposed to the event).\n126. #[macro_export]\n127. macro_rules! metadata_path {\n128.     ($($segment:expr),*) => {{\n129.            ($crate::path::PathPrefix::Metadata, &[$($crate::path::BorrowedSegment::from($segment),)*])\n130.     }};\n131. }\n132. \n133. /// Syntactic sugar for creating a pre-parsed owned path.\n134. ///\n135. /// This allocates and will be slower than using `path!`. Prefer that when possible.\n136. /// The return value must be borrowed to get a value that implements `Path`.\n137. ///\n138. /// Example: `owned_value_path!(\"foo\", 4, \"bar\")` is the pre-parsed path of `foo[4].bar`\n139. #[macro_export]\n140. macro_rules! owned_value_path {\n141. This module contains all of the logic for paths.\n //!\n //! Paths can be thought of as similar to file paths (in an operating system) pointing\n //! to specific files inside of a directory.\n //! A `Value` is a data structure that can contain recursively nested fields. Paths\n //! allow referring to a specific field inside of a `Value`.\n //!\n //! # Example\n //! Below is a sample `Value`. Different fields can be accessed with paths.\n //! ```json\n //! {\n //!   \"foo\": {\n //!       \"bar\": 1\n //!    },\n //!    \"baz\": [\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"]\n //! }\n //! ```\n //!\n //! | path   | value it points to                    |\n //! |--------|---------------------------------------|\n //! | `.foo.bar` | `1`\n //! | `.foo` | `{ \"bar\": 1 }`\n //! | `.`    | `{ \"foo\" : { \"bar\" : 1 }, \"baz\" : [\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"] }`\n //! | `.baz[0]` | `\"a\"`\n //! | `.baz` | `[\"a\", \"b\", \"c\"]`\n //!\n //!\n //! # Traits\n //! There are 2 main traits that define a path. Most functions that use a path for querying\n //! will require one of these traits, rather than a concrete type.\n //!\n //! - [ValuePath] is a path that points to a field inside of a `Value`.\n //! - [TargetPath] is a path that points to a field inside of a `target`. A `target` in VRL refers to\n //! the external data being processed by a VRL script. A `target` has two main sections that can be\n //! pointed to, `event` and `metadata`.  [TargetPath::prefix] identifies the section, and\n //! [TargetPath::value_path] is a [ValuePath] pointing into that section.\n //!\n //! Note that for performance reasons, since [ValuePath] and [TargetPath] require [Clone], these\n //! traits are only implemented on types that are cheap to clone (usually references). That means\n //! when passing in a value (e.g. [OwnedValuePath]) into a function that requires `impl ValuePath`,\n //! it will generally need to be passed in as a reference.\n //!\n //! # Owned Paths\n //! [OwnedValuePath] and [OwnedTargetPath] are pre-parsed paths. That means that accessing fields\n //! using an owned path is very fast. There is an upfront cost however, since owned paths are parsed\n //! when they are created, and the segments are heap allocated. Owned paths should be preferred\n //! if they can be created when performance isn't as much of a concern (e.g. startup time)\n //! and they can be stored for re-use.\n //! Owned paths tend to be easier to work with since you can directly access / manipulate the\n //! segments that make up the path.\n //!\n //! If a path is being created and will only be used once, it may make sense to use other types.\n //! For example here are two different ways to append a segment to a [OwnedValuePath]  before querying\n //! a `Value`:\n //! - Use [OwnedValuePath::with_field_appended] to create a new [OwnedValuePath] and use that. This\n //! method is preferred if the new path will be used multiple times and the path adjustment can be\n //! done in a non performance-critical part of the code (e.g. at startup).\n //! - Use [ValuePath::concat] which con concatenate two [ValuePath]'s very efficiently without\n //! allocating on the heap.\n //!\n //!
